lmsArticle.title: Data Lineage Explained: Tracking Data Flow Across Your Organization
lmsArticle.subtitle: Master the art of tracking data movement, debugging pipelines, and meeting compliance requirements
lmsArticle.excerpt: 📊 Data lineage is the complete genealogy of your data — where it comes from, how it's transformed, and where it ends up. It's critical for debugging pipelines, proving compliance, and understanding data dependencies. Implement it using OpenLineage, Apache Atlas, or custom tracking to prevent silent data failures and meet audit requirements.
lmsArticle.content:
## Scenario context 📊 Data lineage is the complete genealogy of your data — where it comes from, how it's transformed, and where it ends up. It's critical for debugging pipelines, proving compliance, and understanding data dependencies. Implement it using OpenLineage, Apache Atlas, or custom tracking to prevent silent data failures and meet audit requirements. Think of data lineage like supply chain tracking for goods. When you order… This walkthrough focuses on **What is Data Lineage? The Data Supply Chain**. Before making a design choice, clarify: - Think of data lineage like supply chain tracking for goods. - When you order a t-shirt online, you can track it from factory → warehouse → truck → doorstep. - Data lineage does the same: it tracks data from source → transformation → storage → consumption. **Concepts in play:** data-warehousing-lakehouse, graph-traversal-algorithms, spark-data-engineering, caching ## Stage 1 — The Silent Crisis: When Data Disappears Into the Black Box - Three months into the fiscal year, your finance team discovers the revenue report shows $2M more revenue than it actually did. - "Where did this number come from?" No one knows. - The pipeline ran successfully. - The warehouse accepted the data. *Applies **data-warehousing-lakehouse** to the decision above.* **Observable outcome:** The warehouse accepted the data. ## Stage 2 — How Data Lineage Works: The Tracking Mechanism - There are three primary approaches to capturing data lineage: Approach 1: Query/Log Parsing (Passive) Parse database logs, Spark job logs, and SQL queries to infer lineage after the fact. - When a Spark job runs, log the SQL it executes 2. - Parse the SQL to extract table and column references 3. - Build a graph: source table.column → target table.column 4. *Applies **graph-traversal-algorithms** to the decision above.* **Observable outcome:** Build a graph: source table.column → target table.column 4. ## Stage 3 — Visualizing the Data Pipeline: From Source to Report - This diagram shows how data flows through a medallion architecture (bronze → silver → gold), and how lineage tracking instruments each layer to build the complete dependency graph. - How to read this diagram: - The left side shows the traditional data pipeline flow (ingestion → transformation → consumption) - The lineage collector (shown in gray) sits alongside the pipeline and tracks every step - T… *Applies **spark-data-engineering** to the decision above.* ``` graph TD A["📦 Source Systems"] --> B["🔌 Ingestion Layer"] B --> C["⚙️ Bronze Layer"] C --> D["🔄 Transformation Layer"] D --> E["🏛️ Silver Layer"] E --> F["📊 Analytics Layer"] F --> G["📈 BI / Reports / Dashboards"] H["🔍 Lineage Collector
(OpenLineage)"] -.->|tracks all flows| B H -.->|tracks all flows| D H -.->|tracks all flows| E H -.->|tracks all flows| G style A fill:#e8f4f8 style G fill:#fff4e6 style H fill:#f0f0f0 ``` **Observable outcome:** How to read this diagram: - The left side shows the traditional data pipeline flow (ingestion → transformation → consumption) - The lineage collector (shown in gray) sits alongside the pipeline and tracks every step - T… ## Stage 4 — OpenLineage: How Industry Standard Lineage Works in Practice - OpenLineage is an open-source standard (sponsored by Databricks, Collibra, Google) for capturing and sharing lineage metadata. - It's the most practical way to implement lineage across modern data stacks. - What OpenLineage Does OpenLineage defines a standard event format that tools can emit to describe: - Job execution (what ran, when, with what parameters) - Data movement (which tables were inputs, outputs, and transform… - Query "What tables feed into revenue by user?" and you get the entire lineage chain. *Applies **caching** to the decision above.* ```python from openlineage.client.run import RunEvent, RunState from openlineage.client.client import OpenLineageClient import datetime # Initialize OpenLineage client (connects to Airflow, Marquez, or custom backend) client = OpenLineageClient(url="http://localhost:5000") # Define a data transformation job job_name = "user_deduplication" run_id = "run-123" # Create a RunEvent describing what your job does run_event = RunEvent( eventTime=datetime.datetime.now().isoformat(), run={"runId": run_id}, job={"namespace": "data-pipeline", "name": job_name}, eventType=RunState.START, inputs=[ { "namespace": "postgres", "name": "public.raw_users", "facets": { "schema": { "fields": [ {"name": "user_id", "type": "int"}, {"name": "email", "type": "string"}, ] } }, } ], outputs=[ { "namespace": "postgres", "name": "public.users_deduplicated", "facets": { "schema": { "fields": [ {"name": "user_id", "type": "int"}, {"name": "email", "type": "string"}, ] } }, } ], producer="https://github.com/mycompany/data-pipelines", ) # Emit the event to the lineage collector client.emit(run_event) # Now your data pipeline is tracked and visible in: # - Marquez (open-source lineage UI) # - Databricks (Unity Catalog) # - Collibra (enterprise governance platform) ``` ``` raw_users (input) ↓ [user_deduplication job] ↓ users_deduplicated (output) ``` **Observable outcome:** Query "What tables feed into revenue by user?" and you get the entire lineage chain. ## Stage 5 — Practical Implementation Patterns - Pattern 1: Lineage in Airflow DAGs Most Airflow integrations automatically emit lineage when you use SQL operators: When this DAG runs, OpenLineage automatically: 1. - Extracts raw users , raw orders as inputs 3. - Extracts analytics.user metrics as output 4. - Emits a RunEvent with full lineage 5. *Applies **data-warehousing-lakehouse** to the decision above.* ```python from airflow import DAG from airflow.providers.apache.spark.operators.spark_sql import SparkSqlOperator with DAG("daily_user_metrics", start_date="2026-01-01") as dag: transform = SparkSqlOperator( task_id="create_user_metrics", sql=""" SELECT u.user_id, COUNT(*) as purchase_count, SUM(o.amount) as total_spent FROM raw_users u LEFT JOIN raw_orders o ON u.user_id = o.user_id GROUP BY u.user_id """, output_table="analytics.user_metrics" # OpenLineage auto-extracts lineage ) ``` ```python import pandas as pd from openlineage.client import run from datetime import datetime def load_and_deduplicate(): """Load raw users, deduplicate by email, save results.""" # Emit START event with run.RunEventAsContext() as ctx: # Register input ctx.add_input_dataset( namespace="postgres", name="public.raw_users", schema=[("user_id", "int"), ("email", "string"), ("name", "string")] ) # Load data users = pd.read_sql("SELECT * FROM raw_users", conn) # Transform (deduplicate by email, keep first occurrence) deduped = users.drop_duplicates(subset=['email'], keep='first') # Save results deduped.to_sql("users_deduplicated", conn, if_exists='replace') # Register output ctx.add_output_dataset( namespace="postgres", name="public.users_deduplicated", schema=[("user_id", "int"), ("email", "string"), ("name", "string")] ) # When this function runs, lineage is automatically tracked load_and_deduplicate() ``` **Observable outcome:** Emits a RunEvent with full lineage 5. ## Stage 6 — Real-World Example: E-Commerce Revenue Pipeline with Lineage - Imagine you're at an e-commerce company. - Revenue is calculated like this: At step 6, someone notices revenue is 10% lower than expected. - Query: "Show me all transformations that fed into revenue by customer" 2. - See step 5 (clean orders) is the immediate source 3. *Applies **graph-traversal-algorithms** to the decision above.* ``` 1. Orders source system (external) ↓ 2. Ingest to Kafka ↓ 3. Stream to Bronze layer (raw_orders table) ↓ 4. Spark job: Clean/validate orders ↓ 5. Silver layer (clean_orders table) ↓ 6. SQL: Join with customer_dim, calculate revenue ↓ 7. Gold layer (revenue_by_customer table) ↓ 8. BI Dashboard (revenue by region, time period, customer tier) ``` **Observable outcome:** See step 5 (clean orders) is the immediate source 3. ## End-to-end outcome After working through the stages, you should be able to explain: - Don't implement all of technical + business + column-level lineage day one. - Begin with table-level lineage (which tables feed which tables). ## Alternatives considered The source focuses on one primary design. A second architecture is not compared, so no alternative is invented here. ## Failure and degraded modes ### Lineage Trade-offs: Accuracy vs Overhead - **Detection:** Lineage Trade-offs: Accuracy vs Overhead - **User or operator impact:** Lineage Trade-offs: Accuracy vs Overhead

seriesList.name: Data Structures and Algorithms
seriesList.description: Master the core of computer science. This series demystifies Data Structures and Algorithms, from Big O to graph theory. Learn to write efficient, scalable code and ace your technical interviews with confidence.

seriesList.name: Machine Learning Fundamentals
seriesList.description: This series breaks down complex mathematical theories and algorithms into simple, intuitive explanations with practical examples, making AI accessible to everyone from beginners to aspiring data scientists.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: Low-Level Design Guide
seriesList.description: Good architecture is built on a foundation of solid low-level design. This series is a deep dive into the "micro" side of software engineering—focusing on class design, object-oriented principles (SOLID), and tactical design patterns. We explore how to translate requirements into clean, maintainable code, handle concurrency at the component level, and define clear interfaces. Whether you're preparing for LLD interviews or looking to sharpen your day-to-day coding craftsmanship, this guide provides the blueprints for building modular software.

seriesList.name: Architecture Patterns for Production Systems
seriesList.description: High-level design is only half the battle; the other half is surviving production. This series explores the architectural patterns required to build resilient, scalable, and maintainable systems. We dive into the trade-offs of microservices vs. monoliths, event-driven architectures, caching strategies, and data consistency models. Each post focuses on proven patterns that solve common bottlenecks in high-traffic production environments, helping you move from "it works on my machine" to "it works at scale."

seriesList.name: How It Works: Internals Explained
seriesList.description: Ever wondered what actually happens when you trigger a function, commit a transaction, or deploy a container? This series peels back the layers of abstraction to explore the low-level mechanics of modern technology. From database engines and operating system internals to the hidden plumbing of distributed systems, we dive deep into the source code and architectural designs that make complex software work. No magic, just engineering.

seriesList.name: Software Engineering Principles
seriesList.description: Writing code is easy; engineering software that lasts is hard. This series explores the core philosophies and mental models that define professional software development. We go beyond syntax to discuss the timeless principles of modularity, abstraction, testing strategies, and technical debt management. Whether we’re discussing the Zen of Python or the rigors of formal verification, this series provides a high-level perspective on how to think like an engineer, not just a coder.
